los.text: Locate the hard and soft palates, describing their muscular actions and bony components
los.html:
PalateComponentsAction
Hard palate (front 2/3)
  • Palatine processes of the maxillae + horizontal plates of the palatine bones
  • Incisive foramen at the front, greater and lesser palatine foramina at the back
Rigid roof of the mouth; separates mouth from nose; surface for the tongue in speech and swallowing
Soft palate (back 1/3)Muscular fold hanging from the back of the hard palate; palatine aponeurosis (tensor veli palatini tendon); ends in the uvula
  • Elevates to seal off the nasopharynx in swallowing and speech
  • Lowers to close off the mouth (breathing through the nose while chewing)

los.text: Describe the actions of the muscles that move the soft palate and their nerve supply
los.html:
MuscleActionNerve
Levator veli palatiniElevates the soft palateVagus (X) via the pharyngeal plexus
Tensor veli palatiniTenses it; opens the auditory tube (swallowing, yawning)Mandibular nerve (V3) (nerve to medial pterygoid)
PalatoglossusRaises the tongue, narrows the oropharyngeal isthmusVagus (pharyngeal plexus)
PalatopharyngeusRaises the pharynx and larynx, closes the nasopharynxVagus
Musculus uvulaeShortens and raises the uvulaVagus
RuleAll palate muscles are vagus except tensor veli palatini (V3).
Vagus lesion
  • The palate fails to rise on one side and the uvula deviates away from the lesion
  • Nasal speech and nasal regurgitation.
Cleft palatePalatal shelves fail to fuse → feeding problems, speech problems, middle ear effusions (tensor veli palatini can't open the auditory tube).

los.text: Describe the innervation of the hard and soft palates (sensory and motor)
los.html:
RegionSensory nerveBranch of
Hard palate (most)Greater palatine nerveMaxillary (V2) via the pterygopalatine ganglion
Hard palate (behind the incisors)Nasopalatine nerve (incisive foramen)V2
Soft palateLesser palatine nerves (+ IX at the back)V2 (and glossopharyngeal)
MotorVagus via the pharyngeal plexus, except tensor veli palatini (V3).
Taste from the soft palate: facial nerve (greater petrosal) fibres travelling with the lesser palatine nerves.
GlandsParasympathetic secretomotor from VII (greater petrosal → pterygopalatine ganglion).

los.text: Describe the components of the gag reflex
los.html:
ComponentNerve
StimulusTouch to the back of the tongue, tonsillar area or posterior pharyngeal wall
AfferentGlossopharyngeal (IX)
CentreNucleus solitarius → nucleus ambiguus (medulla)
EfferentVagus (X): pharyngeal constrictors and palate muscles contract
  • Testing: touch each side
    • compare.
    • Absent gag with a unilateral IX or X lesion
    • preserved in many people anyway, so it's not a reliable test of swallow safety.

los.text: Describe the general disposition and relationships of the pharynx
los.html:
• Pharynx: fibromuscular tube ~12–15 cm from the skull base to C6 (lower border of the cricoid), where it becomes the oesophagus.
PartLevelLies behindFeatures
NasopharynxSkull base to soft palate (C1)Nasal cavity (choanae)Auditory tube opening, adenoids (pharyngeal tonsil), pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmüller: nasopharyngeal cancer)
OropharynxSoft palate to the epiglottis tip (C2–3)Mouth (oropharyngeal isthmus)Palatine tonsils between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches, back of the tongue, vallecula
Laryngopharynx (hypopharynx)Epiglottis to cricoid (C3–6)LarynxPiriform fossae either side of the laryngeal inlet (foreign bodies, fish bones), postcricoid region
  • Relations: behind = retropharyngeal space, prevertebral fascia, cervical vertebrae
    • sides = carotid sheath, styloid process and muscles, parapharyngeal space, thyroid lobes (lower).

los.text: Identify the opening of the auditory (Eustachian) tube in the nasopharynx
los.html:
Auditory (Eustachian) tube opening
  • on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, ~1 cm behind the inferior nasal concha, surrounded above and behind by the torus tubarius (cartilage ridge).
  • The salpingopharyngeal fold runs down from it
  • The pharyngeal recess lies behind.
FunctionEqualises middle ear pressure and drains the middle ear; opened by tensor veli palatini (and levator) on swallowing and yawning.
Clinical
  • Children have a shorter, more horizontal tube → otitis media
  • Enlarged adenoids block it (glue ear)
  • a unilateral middle ear effusion in an adult needs the nasopharynx checked for cancer.

los.text: List the constrictor muscles of the pharynx
los.html:
MuscleOriginDetail
Superior constrictorPterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, mandibleTop edge leaves a gap below the skull base (auditory tube, levator veli palatini pass)
Middle constrictorHyoid (greater and lesser horns), stylohyoid ligament
Inferior constrictorThyropharyngeus (thyroid cartilage) and cricopharyngeus (cricoid)Cricopharyngeus = upper oesophageal sphincter
InsertionAll into the pharyngeal raphe at the back (midline).
ArrangementThey overlap like stacked cups (inferior outside middle outside superior) and squeeze food down in sequence.
Longitudinal musclesStylopharyngeus (IX), palatopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus (X): elevate the pharynx and larynx in swallowing.
NerveAll constrictors: vagus via the pharyngeal plexus (cricopharyngeus also from the recurrent laryngeal).

los.text: Describe the mucosa, fascia and tissue spaces of the pharynx and explain the condition quinsy
los.html:
Layer (inside → out)Detail
MucosaPseudostratified ciliated (nasopharynx); stratified squamous (oro- and laryngopharynx)
Pharyngobasilar fasciaThick submucosa, especially above the superior constrictor
MuscleConstrictors + longitudinal muscles
Buccopharyngeal fasciaThin outer layer
SpaceLocationClinical
PeritonsillarBetween the tonsil capsule and the superior constrictorQuinsy
RetropharyngealBehind the buccopharyngeal fascia, in front of the prevertebral fasciaAbscess in children; spread to the mediastinum
ParapharyngealBeside the pharynx (skull base to hyoid)Spread from tonsil/teeth; carotid sheath at risk
  • Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess): a complication of tonsillitis
    • pus between the tonsil capsule and superior constrictor.
    • Signs: severe one-sided sore throat, trismus (medial pterygoid irritated), "hot potato" voice, uvula pushed to the opposite side, drooling, ear pain (IX).
    • Treatment: needle aspiration or incision and drainage, antibiotics.

los.text: Explain the innervation of the pharynx
los.html:
• Pharyngeal plexus: on the middle constrictor, formed by IX (sensory), X (motor) and sympathetic fibres (superior cervical ganglion).
PartSensoryMotor
NasopharynxMaxillary (V2) (pharyngeal branch)
OropharynxGlossopharyngeal (IX)Vagus (X) for all muscles except stylopharyngeus (IX)
LaryngopharynxVagus (X) (internal laryngeal nerve)Vagus (and recurrent laryngeal for cricopharyngeus)
  • Referred ear pain: IX and X also supply the ear (tympanic nerve, auricular branch), so tonsillitis, quinsy and throat cancers cause otalgia.

los.text: List the structures passing through the walls of pharynx
los.html:
GapBetweenStructures passing through
Above the superior constrictorSkull base and superior constrictorAuditory tube, levator veli palatini, ascending palatine artery
Between superior and middle constrictorsStylopharyngeus, glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), stylohyoid ligament, lingual nerve (nearby)
Between middle and inferior constrictorsInternal laryngeal nerve, superior laryngeal artery and vein (pierce the thyrohyoid membrane)
Below the inferior constrictorRecurrent laryngeal nerve, inferior laryngeal artery

los.text: Describe the cricopharyngeal sphincter (or upper oesophageal sphincter)
los.html:
Cricopharyngeus
  • Lower part of the inferior constrictor, horizontal fibres from one side of the cricoid to the other, at C6
  • The upper oesophageal sphincter and narrowest part of the gut tube (~15 cm from the teeth).
FunctionTonically contracted at rest (stops air entering the oesophagus during inspiration and reflux into the pharynx); relaxes briefly during swallowing.
Killian's dehiscence
  • Weak area between thyropharyngeus (oblique) and cricopharyngeus (horizontal)
  • at the back → pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) in older people: dysphagia
  • Regurgitation of undigested food
  • Halitosis
  • Gurgling neck swelling (usually left).
  • Risk of perforation at endoscopy.
NerveVagus via the pharyngeal plexus and recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Foreign bodies (coins, food boluses) often stick here.

los.text: Recognise the anatomical arrangement of the lymphoid tissue of the pharynx (Waldeyer's tonsillar ring)
los.html:
• Waldeyer's ring: a ring of lymphoid tissue guarding the entrance to the aerodigestive tract.
TonsilPosition
Pharyngeal (adenoids)Roof and back wall of the nasopharynx
Tubal (×2)Around the auditory tube openings
Palatine (×2)Oropharynx, in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
LingualBack third of the tongue
Clinical
  • Enlarged adenoids → mouth breathing, snoring, sleep apnoea, glue ear
  • Palatine tonsils → tonsillitis, quinsy, obstructive sleep apnoea.
  • Tonsillectomy bleeding comes from the paratonsillar (external palatine) vein and tonsillar branch of the facial artery
  • The glossopharyngeal nerve lies in the tonsil bed (post-operative ear pain and taste changes).
Lymph drainageto the jugulodigastric node.
AtrophyThe ring shrinks after childhood.

los.text: Identify the hyoid bone, the cartilaginous skeleton and ligamentous structures of the larynx
los.html:
StructureDetail
Hyoid (C3)U-shaped bone, body and greater/lesser horns; not part of the larynx but the larynx hangs from it; no bony joints
Thyroid cartilage (hyaline)Two laminae meeting at the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple); superior and inferior horns
Cricoid cartilage (hyaline, C6)Only complete ring in the airway; signet-ring shape (taller behind)
Arytenoid cartilages (×2, hyaline)On the top of the cricoid lamina; vocal process (vocal ligament attaches) and muscular process
Epiglottis (elastic)Leaf-shaped, behind the tongue, attached to the thyroid cartilage
Corniculate and cuneiform (elastic)Small, in the aryepiglottic folds
Membrane / ligamentJoins
Thyrohyoid membraneHyoid and thyroid cartilage (pierced by the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels)
Cricothyroid membrane (cricothyroid ligament)Thyroid and cricoid; its free upper edge is the vocal ligament (conus elasticus)
Quadrangular membraneEpiglottis and arytenoids; lower free edge = vestibular ligament (false cord)
Cricotracheal ligamentCricoid and first tracheal ring
  • Joints: cricothyroid (synovial: thyroid tilts forward on the cricoid) and cricoarytenoid (synovial: arytenoids rotate and glide).

los.text: Demonstrate the palpable positions of the hyoid bone, thyroid and cricoid cartilages
los.html:
• From the chin down in the midline:
1. Hyoid bone(C3)Just above the thyroid cartilage, in the angle between chin and neck; moves up on swallowing.
2. Thyroid notch and laryngeal prominence(C4)Most obvious in men.
3. Cricothyroid membranea soft dip between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages: site of emergency cricothyroidotomy (few vessels, below the vocal cords).
4. Cricoid cartilage(C6)Firm ring below the dip; pressure here (cricoid pressure) was used to compress the oesophagus during rapid sequence induction.
5Tracheal rings and the thyroid isthmus (rings 2–4).

los.text: Describe the muscles that elevate the larynx and facilitate closure of the inlet
los.html:
ActionMusclesNerve
Elevating the larynx (swallowing)Suprahyoid: mylohyoid, geniohyoid, digastric, stylohyoid; thyrohyoid; longitudinal pharyngeal muscles (stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus)V3 (mylohyoid, anterior digastric), VII (posterior digastric, stylohyoid), C1 (geniohyoid, thyrohyoid), IX, X
Closing the inletAryepiglottic and oblique arytenoid muscles (sphincter); thyroepiglottic; larynx rising under the tongue base tips the epiglottis backRecurrent laryngeal (X)
Depressing the larynx (after swallowing)Infrahyoid strap musclesAnsa cervicalis (C1–3)
  • Protecting the airway in swallowing: breathing stops
    • the larynx rises and moves forward
    • the inlet and vocal folds close
    • and the epiglottis folds down over the inlet.

los.text: Describe the intrinsic laryngeal muscles responsible for controlling vocal cord position and tension and how these function during phonation, laryngeal closure, the cough reflex and regulation of intrathoracic pressure
los.html:
MuscleAction on the vocal cordsNerve
Posterior cricoarytenoidThe only abductor (opens the rima glottidis)Recurrent laryngeal
Lateral cricoarytenoidAdducts (closes)Recurrent laryngeal
Transverse and oblique arytenoidsAdduct (close the back of the glottis)Recurrent laryngeal
CricothyroidTenses (lengthens) the cords: higher pitchExternal laryngeal (superior laryngeal)
Thyroarytenoid / vocalisRelaxes (shortens) and fine-tunes tensionRecurrent laryngeal
SituationWhat the larynx does
PhonationCords adducted and tensed; air forced through makes them vibrate (pitch from tension and length, loudness from air pressure)
Laryngeal closure (swallowing)Cords, vestibular folds and inlet all close
CoughCords close, expiratory muscles build pressure, then cords open suddenly to blast air out
Effort closure (Valsalva)Cords close to raise intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure (lifting, straining, defecation, childbirth) and fix the chest
Quiet breathingCords partly abducted
Deep breathingCords fully abducted (posterior cricoarytenoid)

los.text: Recognise the chambers of the larynx
los.html:
ChamberBetweenFeatures
Vestibule (supraglottis)Laryngeal inlet → vestibular folds (false cords)Aryepiglottic folds, epiglottis
Ventricle (with saccule)Between the vestibular and vocal foldsMucous glands lubricate the cords
Infraglottic cavity (subglottis)Vocal folds → lower border of cricoidContinuous with the trachea; narrowest part of the airway in young children
Rima glottidisGap between the vocal folds (narrowest part of the adult airway).
GlottisThe vocal folds + rima glottidis.

los.text: List the functions of the larynx
los.html:
Protects the airway(sphincter; most important function)Closes in swallowing, cough reflex.
BreathingAn open, adjustable airway.
PhonationVoice production.
Effort closureRaises intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure (Valsalva) for lifting, coughing, defecating, childbirth.
CoughExpels foreign material and secretions.

los.text: Describe the origin, course and functions of the motor and sensory nerve supplies of the larynx and the functional consequences of injury to these nerves
los.html:
NerveOrigin and courseMotorSensory
Superior laryngealVagus at the inferior ganglion → down beside the pharynx → splits
↳ Internal laryngealPierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal arteryNoneMucosa above the vocal cords (cough reflex afferent)
↳ External laryngealRuns down with the superior thyroid arteryCricothyroidNone
Recurrent laryngeal
  • Right: hooks under the right subclavian artery
  • Left: under the aortic arch (by the ligamentum arteriosum)
  • → up in the tracheo-oesophageal groove
  • → enters the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint
All other intrinsic musclesMucosa below the vocal cords
InjuryCauseResult
External laryngealThyroidectomy (tying the superior thyroid artery)Weak, monotonous voice; can't reach high notes
Internal laryngealRareLoss of sensation above the cords → aspiration
One recurrent laryngealThyroidectomy, lung cancer or aortic aneurysm (left), oesophageal cancer, central linesHoarse voice; affected cord lies near the midline (paramedian)
Both recurrent laryngealThyroidectomyBoth cords near the midline → stridor, airway obstruction (may need tracheostomy)
  • Left RLN is longer (goes down into the chest), so it's damaged more often.

los.text: Recall and recognise the arterial supply, venous and lymphatic drainage of the larynx
los.html:
Above the vocal cordsBelow the vocal cords
ArteriesSuperior laryngeal artery (superior thyroid → ECA)Inferior laryngeal artery (inferior thyroid → thyrocervical trunk)
VeinsSuperior laryngeal vein → superior thyroid → IJVInferior laryngeal vein → inferior thyroid → brachiocephalic
LymphUpper deep cervical nodesPre-laryngeal, pre-tracheal and paratracheal nodes → lower deep cervical
  • Vocal folds have very little lymphatic drainage, so glottic cancers spread late (and present early with hoarseness: good prognosis).
    • Supraglottic cancers spread early, often to both sides.

los.text: Demonstrate on a model how the larynx works during breathing and phonation, noting that it opens during breathing and is partially closed during speaking
los.html:
Breathing
  • The posterior cricoarytenoids rotate the arytenoids outwards so the vocal processes swing apart
  • The rima glottidis opens into a wide triangle (wider still in deep breaths).
Speaking
  • Lateral cricoarytenoids and arytenoid muscles bring the vocal processes together so the rima is nearly closed
  • Cricothyroid tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to stretch the cords
  • Air pressure from below forces the cords apart in rapid vibrations.
WhisperingThe front of the cords close but a small triangular gap stays open at the back between the arytenoids.
PitchLonger, tighter cords (cricothyroid) and a higher vibration rate give a higher pitch.

los.text: Recognise structures of the larynx and pharynx on radiographs
